title: The Last Stretch of the Road
sum: Jesus leaves Galilee for Judea. Pharisees test him on divorce, and he answers that God made male and female and joined them, so that divorce goes against God's purpose; in the house he tells the disciples that a man or a woman who divorces and remarries commits adultery (10:1–12). He welcomes the children the disciples tried to keep away (10:13–16). A man runs up to ask how to inherit eternal life; Jesus looks at him, loves him, and tells him to sell what he has and follow. The man leaves in grief, and Jesus tells the stunned disciples how hard it is for the rich to enter the kingdom, though with God all things are possible (10:17–31).

On the road up to Jerusalem Jesus foretells his death and rising for the third time (10:32–34). James and John ask for the seats at his right and left in his glory; he asks whether they can drink his cup and share his baptism, and teaches all twelve that greatness means being a servant and slave, "for the Son of Man, too, did not come to have people serve him" but to give his life as a ransom in place of many (10:35–45). At Jericho blind Bartimaeus calls him Son of David, throws off his cloak, receives his sight and follows him on the road (10:46–52).
readings: Read as a lesson in discipleship

The chapter closes the long section on "the road" (8:27–10:52), in which Jesus three times foretells his death and three times the disciples misunderstand (9:33–34; 10:35–37). Each time he answers with teaching on the last being first. Read this way, the children, the rich man, James and John, and Bartimaeus are four pictures of what it means to receive the kingdom and follow.

Marriage, children, property and power were the four pillars of status in the ancient household. Jesus speaks to each: the husband may not discard his wife, children are welcomed, property is to be given away, and rulers are to be slaves. Read this way, the chapter is a picture of a new household, the community of disciples (10:29–30).
Read as the meaning of the cross

10:45 is Mark's clearest word on why Jesus dies. Read this way, the whole chapter leads up to it: the cup and the baptism (10:38), the third prediction (10:33–34), and the ransom. The blind man who sees and follows (10:52) is the reader's model, set against disciples who see Jesus every day and do not understand.

views.H: Jesus now travels through Judea, under the Roman governor, and the land beyond the Jordan, Perea, ruled by Herod Antipas. Mark does not say where the divorce debate took place; if it was in Antipas' territory, the question was dangerous there, since John the Baptist had died over Antipas' marriage to Herodias (6:17–29). Jericho, a rich oasis with a Herodian palace, was the last stop for Galilean pilgrims before the climb to Jerusalem for Passover. Rich landowners, tenant farmers and beggars all appear in this chapter, as they did on the roads of Roman Palestine.
views.C: Matthew follows this chapter closely (Matthew 19:1–20:34) but makes several changes that scholars use in the debate over which Gospel came first: the exception clause on divorce (Matthew 19:9), "Why do you call me good?" (10:18) becoming "Why are you asking me about the good?" (Matthew 19:17), the mother who asks for her sons (Matthew 20:20), and two blind men instead of one named Bartimaeus (Matthew 20:30). Most scholars hold that Matthew is revising Mark; supporters of the Two-Gospel hypothesis argue that Mark shortened and combined Matthew and Luke. The saying on a wife who divorces (10:12) is often taken as Mark's application of Jesus' teaching to Roman law, though some think Jesus himself may have meant Herodias.
views.L: The chapter completes Mark's central section, framed by two healings of blind men (8:22–26; 10:46–52), in which three predictions of the passion (8:31; 9:31; 10:33–34) are each followed by the disciples' failure and Jesus' teaching. The same question, "What would you like me to do for you?" is put to James and John (10:36) and to Bartimaeus (10:51): the brothers ask for glory, the blind man for sight. The places "on your right and on your left" (10:37, 40) return at the cross (15:27).
views.J: Every scene is at home in first-century Judaism. Teachers debated the grounds of divorce (Mishnah Gittin 9:10), and the Damascus Document used Genesis 1:27 as Jesus does. The rich man's question about inheriting eternal life is a Jewish question, and Jesus answers from the Ten Commandments. Jewish scholars such as Amy-Jill Levine point out that later Christian contrasts between "Jewish legalism" and Jesus' teaching misread a passage where Jesus sends a Jew back to the Torah and then asks more.
views.T: The church fathers read 10:45 as the heart of the gospel, and the debate over to whom the ransom was paid runs from Origen to Gregory of Nazianzus. 10:17–22 inspired the monastic movement: Athanasius tells how Antony heard "go, sell" read in church and gave away his land (Life of Antony 2). Western law and most Protestant churches came to allow divorce in limited cases, while the Catholic Church holds sacramental marriage indissoluble, with Mark's unqualified form of the saying as a key text. "Son of David, have mercy on me" became the root of the Jesus Prayer.

deep.b:
Chapter 10 closes Mark's central section, the teaching Jesus gives "on the road" between two healings of blind men (8:22–26; 10:46–52). Its design, three predictions of the passion each followed by a misunderstanding and a teaching, is set out in the deep dive on Mark 8 ("Two blind men frame the road") and the note on 8:27.

What chapter 10 adds is the climax. The third prediction is the fullest: the Son of Man will be handed over to the Gentiles, mocked, spat on and flogged (10:33–34). The third misunderstanding is the boldest: James and John ask for the seats of honor in his glory (10:35–37). And the third teaching ends with the verse that explains all three predictions: the Son of Man came to serve and to give his life as a ransom in place of many (10:45). Then the same question, "What would you like me to do for you?" (10:36, 51), is put to the brothers and to a blind beggar. They ask for glory; he asks for sight, receives it at once, and follows Jesus on the road. Many commentators, such as Morna Hooker and Joel Marcus, read the contrast as Mark's word to his church: the one who sees is the one who follows.

deep.title: Claude's theory: a trail of garments
deep.b: Mark returns several times to people and their outer garments, and the pattern may be deliberate. The rich man will not give up his property (10:22). Bartimaeus throws away his cloak, perhaps all he owns, to come to Jesus (10:50). The crowd spreads their cloaks on the road for a king (11:8). In the end, a young man runs away naked, leaving his linen cloth behind (14:51–52), and the soldiers divide Jesus' own clothes (15:24). Read in sequence, the garments trace what following Jesus costs: some keep what they have, some throw it off, and finally Jesus himself is stripped. Literary critics have commented on several of these garment scenes, especially the young man and Bartimaeus; linking all five as a chain is this site's suggestion.

echoes: Genesis 1:27; Genesis 2:24; Deuteronomy 24:1–4; Exodus 20:12–16; Isaiah 53:10–12; Daniel 7:13–14; Psalm 75:8; Isaiah 51:17; 8:22–26; 8:31; 9:31; 15:27; Matthew 19:1–20:34; Luke 18:15–43; 1 Corinthians 7:10–11; 1 Timothy 2:6

settings.to: Pharisees who came to test him, with the crowd listening
settings.when: on the way to Jerusalem, probably in Perea (Antipas' territory) or in Judea; Mark does not say where
settings.why: The Pharisees want to see whether Jesus will openly reject the permission in Deuteronomy 24. He answers by going behind Moses to creation: God's purpose for marriage is that two become one, and the permission was a concession to hard hearts. The rule at stake is the Torah itself, as all Jewish schools read it, not a Pharisaic tradition: every school allowed divorce; they differed on the grounds. If the debate took place in Antipas' territory, the fact that he had killed John over his marriage shows why the question was a trap. Matthew sets the debate on the same journey (Matthew 19:1–9).
settings.readers: Mark's church, in a Roman world where divorce was easy for both husband and wife, heard that the Christian household is bound by God's original purpose, not by the law of the land.

settings.what: The private teaching on divorce and remarriage
settings.to: the disciples, privately, in the house
settings.when: after the public debate
settings.why: To spell out what the public answer means: remarriage after divorce is adultery, whether the husband or the wife ends the marriage. The second half, about a wife who divorces, fits Roman and Greek law, not Jewish law, under which only husbands could divorce. Matthew has no private scene: the saying, with its exception clause, ends the public answer to the Pharisees (Matthew 19:9). The same teaching also stands in the Sermon on the Mount (Matthew 5:32) and in a string of sayings to the Pharisees in Luke 16:18.
settings.readers: For Mark's readers in the Roman world, 10:12 applied the teaching to wives who had the legal right to divorce their husbands.
views: Many scholars think Mark (or the church before him) extended Jesus' saying to fit Roman law, as Paul also speaks to wives (1 Corinthians 7:10–13).
Others suggest Jesus could have meant Herodias, who left her husband to marry Antipas, or Jewish women in Gentile cities.

settings.to: the disciples who were turning the children away, and the people bringing the children
settings.when: on the road in Judea
settings.why: To correct the disciples, who thought children unimportant, and to teach that the kingdom of God is received as a gift by those with no claims, like children.
settings.readers: Mark's church, meeting in households with children and slaves, learned that no one is too small for Jesus; later churches heard in it a word about bringing infants to baptism.

settings.what: The conversation with the rich man
settings.to: a man who ran up and knelt, with the disciples present
settings.when: as Jesus set out on the road
settings.why: The man asks sincerely how to inherit eternal life. Jesus points him to the commandments about other people, then, out of love, names the one thing holding him back: his wealth. The call to sell and follow is a call to discipleship like that of the fishermen (1:16–20).
settings.readers: Mark's readers, some of whom had given up property and families (10:28–30), saw their choice in his; those who had kept their wealth heard a warning.
views: Many, including most Protestant interpreters, take the command as addressed to this man, whose wealth was his idol.
Catholic and Orthodox tradition read it as a counsel of perfection, taken up by monks and religious (see the card on Matthew 19:21).

settings.what: The teaching on wealth and reward
settings.to: the disciples, with Peter speaking for them
settings.when: just after the rich man leaves
settings.why: To shock the disciples out of the belief that wealth is a sign of God's favor and an advantage in reaching the kingdom, and then to promise those who had left everything a new family now and eternal life later.
settings.readers: "With persecutions" (10:30) spoke directly to a church that had lost homes and families for the gospel, whether in Rome after AD 64 or in Syria and Galilee during the Jewish war.

settings.what: The third prediction of the passion
settings.to: the Twelve, taken aside from the others on the road
settings.when: on the road up to Jerusalem, with Jesus walking ahead
settings.why: To prepare his closest followers, again and in the fullest detail, for his rejection, death and rising, so that they would understand that he goes to it on purpose.
settings.readers: Mark's readers, who knew the end, saw that every step had been foretold, and that the cross was not a defeat.

settings.what: The request of James and John and the teaching on greatness
settings.to: James and John, then all twelve disciples
settings.when: on the road, right after the third prediction
settings.why: To expose the ambition of the Twelve, to warn James and John that sharing his glory means sharing his cup and baptism, and to give the rule for leadership among his followers: serve, as the Son of Man came to serve and to give his life as a ransom. In Matthew the brothers' mother makes the request (Matthew 20:20); Luke has no request, and sets the teaching on greatness at the Last Supper (Luke 22:24–27).
settings.readers: In Mark's church, which had leaders and members of every social level, this was the charter of Christian leadership. James had already died a martyr (Acts 12:2), and the prediction about the cup was known to have come true for James.

settings.to: Jesus, in front of the crowd leaving Jericho
settings.when: on the last stage of the journey, before the climb to Jerusalem
settings.why: The blind beggar is the first to call Jesus "Son of David," naming him as the royal Messiah just before he enters David's city. Jesus' question, the same he asked James and John (10:36), lets him ask for sight, not glory. Matthew tells of two blind men as Jesus left Jericho (Matthew 20:29–34); Luke places the healing as Jesus approached the town (Luke 18:35).
settings.readers: Mark's readers saw in the man who received sight and "followed him on the road" a picture of their own conversion and calling.

traditions.q: Jesus came "to give his life as a ransom in place of many" (10:45). How does his death save, and for whom?
views: The ransom frees humanity from death, corruption and the devil's power; Christ conquers death by death and opens the way to union with God (theosis). The fathers refused to say the ransom was paid to the Father as though he needed it: Gregory of Nazianzus asks to whom the price was paid and answers that the Father did not demand it (Oration 45.22).

Christ's death is the sacrifice that "atoned for our faults and made satisfaction for our sins to the Father" (Catechism 615), offered out of love for all people without exception (Catechism 605). Aquinas explains it as satisfaction, sacrifice and redemption together, building on Anselm.

Christ truly suffered and died "that he might reconcile the Father unto us, and be a sacrifice not only for original guilt, but also for all actual sins" (Augsburg Confession 3). He bore God's wrath and curse in our place, for all people, and the benefit is received by faith.

Christ bore "the wrath of God against the sin of the whole human race" (Heidelberg Catechism 37) as the substitute for sinners, satisfying God's justice. Many Reformed teachers, following the Canons of Dort (2.8) and Westminster (8.5), hold that the atonement was designed to save effectually the elect, so "many" is not "all."

Christ's offering, once made, "is that perfect redemption, propitiation, and satisfaction, for all the sins of the whole world, both original and actual" (Thirty-Nine Articles, Article 31). Anglicans have held both a general atonement and, among some Calvinist Anglicans, a limited one; the Articles themselves speak of the whole world.

The Methodist Articles of Religion keep the Anglican wording on Christ's offering "for all the sins of the whole world" (Article 20). Wesley insisted that Christ died for all, not only for the elect (compare 1 Timothy 2:6), and that anyone may receive the benefit by faith.

Divided on "for whom." Particular Baptists teach that Christ's death was designed to redeem those the Father gave him, and that it surely saves all of them (Second London Confession 8.5, 8.8). General Baptists, including Free Will Baptists, teach that Christ died for every person and that the benefit is received by faith. The Baptist Faith and Message says that by his substitutionary death Christ made provision for the redemption of people from sin (Article II.B), and Southern Baptists hold both views under it.

Mennonite and other Anabaptist teaching has long used several pictures of the cross together. Some recent Mennonite theologians, such as J. Denny Weaver, reject satisfaction and penal views and read the cross as God's nonviolent victory over the powers ("narrative Christus Victor"); others in the tradition keep substitution. The tradition is divided.

title: The King, the Fig Tree and the Temple
sum: Near the Mount of Olives Jesus sends two disciples for a colt no one has ridden. He rides it toward Jerusalem while the crowd spreads cloaks and greenery on the road and shouts "Hosanna! Blessed is the one who comes in the Lord's name! Blessed is our father David's kingdom, which is coming!" He enters the temple, looks around at everything, and, since it is late, goes out to Bethany (11:1–11).

The next morning he looks for figs on a leafy tree and finds none, though it is not fig season, and says no one will ever eat fruit from it again. In the temple he throws out the sellers and buyers, overturns the tables of the money changers, and teaches that God's house was to be "a house of prayer for all the nations," but they have made it a cave for bandits. The chief priests and scribes begin looking for a way to destroy him (11:12–19). The following morning the fig tree has withered from the roots, and Jesus speaks of faith, prayer and forgiveness (11:20–25). The chief priests, scribes and elders challenge his authority; he answers with a question about John's baptism, and they refuse to answer (11:27–33).
readings: Read as the coming of the king

Jesus enters as a king in the manner of Zechariah 9:9, on a colt, welcomed with Psalm 118. Read this way, the chapter is the Messiah's claim on his city and his temple, made in the humble way the prophets foretold.
Read as a sign of judgment on the temple

The fig tree wrapped around the temple scene interprets it: the temple, like the leafy tree, looks alive but bears no fruit, and it will wither. Read this way, Jesus' action is not a cleansing but an acted prophecy of destruction, as Jeremiah's was (Jeremiah 7; 19), fulfilled in AD 70 (13:2).
Read as a renewal of prayer

Jesus quotes Isaiah's promise of a house of prayer for all the nations, and then teaches the disciples to pray with faith and to forgive. Read this way, the chapter moves the center of prayer from a building to a praying, forgiving community, open to Gentiles.

views.H: Passover crowds swelled Jerusalem many times over, and the Roman governor came up from Caesarea with troops to keep order. The temple, rebuilt on a vast scale by Herod the Great and still being finished, was the center of Jewish worship and of the city's economy. Its outer court held the market for sacrificial animals and the changing of money for the half-shekel tax (Mishnah Shekalim 1:3). Any disturbance there at Passover was dangerous, and E. P. Sanders argued that this act, more than any other, led to Jesus' arrest.
views.C: Mark spreads the events over three days (11:11, 12, 20); Matthew puts the temple action on the day of the entry and tells the fig tree story in one piece afterward (Matthew 21:12–22); Luke has no fig tree cursing; John places the temple action at the start of Jesus' ministry (John 2:13–22). Most scholars think one temple incident lies behind all four, though some think there were two. The cursing of the fig tree is often taken as Mark's own symbolic framing, perhaps built from a parable like Luke 13:6–9. Those who date Mark after AD 70 see the withered tree as a comment on the temple's fall; those who date it before see a prophecy.
views.L: 11:12–25 is one of Mark's "sandwiches": fig tree, temple, fig tree. Each half explains the other: the temple is the fruitless tree, and the withered tree is the temple's fate. The unanswered question about authority (11:27–33) opens a series of five controversies in the temple that run to 12:37, mirroring the five controversies in Galilee (2:1–3:6). The crowd's welcome of "David's kingdom" (11:10) sets up Jesus' question about David's son (12:35–37).
views.J: Jesus acts as a Jewish prophet in the temple, not as an outsider attacking Judaism: he quotes Isaiah and Jeremiah, and he forbids using the temple as a shortcut, as the Mishnah also does (Mishnah Berakhot 9:5). Jewish scholars such as Paula Fredriksen note that the trade was required for the sacrifices the Torah commands, so the act was not a protest against "Jewish ritual" as such. Other Jews also criticized the priestly leadership, including the Qumran community and later rabbinic texts that remember the high-priestly houses as greedy (Babylonian Talmud, Pesachim 57a).
views.T: The church celebrates the entry on Palm Sunday, from at least the 300s in Jerusalem, as the pilgrim Egeria describes. "Hosanna" and "Blessed is he who comes" entered every ancient liturgy as the Sanctus. The cleansing of the temple was read by the fathers as a picture of Christ cleansing the soul, the church, and the clergy from simony; reformers from Hus to Luther used it against the sale of indulgences. The cursing of the fig tree was read as a parable in action against fruitless faith.

deep.h: Why did Jesus act in the temple?
deep.b:
The three standard explanations, a cleansing of abuses, a sign of the temple's destruction (E. P. Sanders), and a reform of the temple's worship, are set out in the deep dive on Matthew 21 ("Why did Jesus overturn the tables?"). Mark's telling adds several things of its own.

The fig tree around it. Mark wraps the scene in the fig tree story (11:12–14, 20–21), so that each half explains the other: the leafy temple bears no fruit and will wither. The saying about "this mountain" (11:23), spoken within sight of the temple mount, points the same way, and Jesus is later accused of threatening to destroy the temple (14:58).

No vessels through the temple. Only Mark says Jesus would not let anyone carry a vessel through the temple (11:16), stopping its use as a shortcut, as the Mishnah also forbids (Mishnah Berakhot 9:5). That is a concern for the place's holiness, not only for its trade.

"For all the nations." Only Mark keeps the end of Isaiah 56:7 (11:17). The market filled the only court where Gentiles could pray, so the act defends their place, a theme Mark's Gentile readers would welcome.

A challenge to the priestly leaders. Some, such as Richard Horsley and Ched Myers, read it as a challenge to the high-priestly families who cooperated with Rome and profited from the temple economy.

Paula Fredriksen has doubted that so small an action, in a court many acres in size, could have halted anything. Most scholars think something happened, and that it was the event that set the authorities against Jesus (11:18).

echoes: Zechariah 9:9; Genesis 49:11; 2 Kings 9:13; Psalm 118:25–26; Malachi 3:1; Isaiah 56:7; Jeremiah 7:11; Jeremiah 8:13; Hosea 9:10; Micah 7:1; Zechariah 14:4; Zechariah 14:21; Matthew 21:1–27; Luke 19:28–20:8; John 2:13–22; John 12:12–19; 13:1–2; 14:58

settings.to: two of his disciples
settings.when: near Bethphage and Bethany, as the group approached Jerusalem
settings.why: To arrange a royal and sacred mount for his entry, one never ridden. The detailed instructions, and the way things happen just as he says, show Jesus in control of what follows.
settings.readers: Mark's readers saw that Jesus entered Jerusalem knowing and choosing what would happen there.

settings.by: the crowd walking in front of Jesus and behind him
settings.to: Jesus, and God
settings.when: on the road down the Mount of Olives toward the city, at Passover time
settings.why: Pilgrims sang Psalm 118 on the way to the feast. Applying "Blessed is the one who comes" to Jesus and hailing "our father David's kingdom," the crowd expresses the hope that he will restore Israel as king.
settings.readers: Mark's readers knew that the king the crowd welcomed would be crowned with thorns, and that his kingdom was not the one they expected.

settings.what: The curse on the fig tree
settings.to: the fig tree, with the disciples listening
settings.when: on the road from Bethany the morning after the entry
settings.why: An acted sign, like the prophets' symbolic acts: the leafy tree with no fruit pictures the temple, busy with worship but without the fruit God looks for. The disciples overhear so that they can grasp its meaning the next day.
settings.readers: For readers who knew of, or feared, the temple's destruction, the withered tree explained it as judgment foretold by Jesus.

settings.what: The action and teaching in the temple
settings.to: the sellers, buyers and money changers, and the people in the temple's outer court
settings.when: the day after the entry, in the days before Passover
settings.why: To protest, in the manner of Jeremiah, against what the temple had become, and to announce God's judgment and his purpose that it be a house of prayer for all the nations. Whose rule was at stake: the trade itself was lawful and served the Torah's sacrifices; Jesus challenges the way the temple was run and the trust placed in it. Matthew sets the action on the day of the entry (Matthew 21:12); John places it at the start of Jesus' ministry (John 2:13–22).
settings.readers: Mark's Gentile readers heard that God's house was meant for them too, and, if they read after AD 70, why it had fallen.
views: Jesus purifies the temple of abuse.
Jesus acts out the temple's coming end (Sanders).

settings.what: Sayings on faith, prayer and forgiveness
settings.to: Peter and the disciples
settings.when: the next morning, beside the withered fig tree
settings.why: To answer Peter's surprise with teaching on faith in God, bold prayer, and the forgiveness that must go with prayer. Coming after the temple scene, the sayings point to prayer that does not depend on the temple. Matthew has the faith saying at the same fig tree (Matthew 21:21–22) but puts the saying on forgiveness in the Sermon on the Mount (Matthew 6:14–15); Luke gives the faith saying elsewhere, about a mulberry tree (Luke 17:6).
settings.readers: Mark's church, without a temple and soon with no hope of one, learned that faithful, forgiving prayer was its access to God.

settings.by: the chief priests, scribes and elders, and Jesus
settings.to: Jesus, in the temple courts, and he to them
settings.when: the third day, while he walked in the temple
settings.why: The leaders, responsible for the temple, ask a fair question: who authorized his action? Jesus' counter-question about John's baptism exposes that they will not commit themselves on a prophet the people accepted, and implies that his authority, like John's, is from heaven.
settings.readers: For Mark's readers, the scene showed that Jesus' authority came from God, as his baptism by John had shown (1:9–11).

title: Questions in the Temple
sum: Jesus tells the chief priests, scribes and elders a parable: a man plants a vineyard and leases it to farmers, who beat and kill the slaves he sends and finally his dearly loved son. The owner will destroy them and give the vineyard to others, and the rejected stone becomes the head of the corner. The leaders know it is aimed at them, but fear the crowd (12:1–12). Pharisees and Herodians ask whether to pay the tax to Caesar; looking at a denarius, Jesus tells them to pay back to Caesar what is Caesar's and to God what is God's (12:13–17). Sadducees, who deny the resurrection, mock it with a story of seven brothers; Jesus answers that the raised are like angels and that God is the God of the living (12:18–27).

A scribe asks which commandment is first. Jesus answers with the Shema, "Listen, Israel: The Lord is our God. The Lord is one," and the command to love God with all one's heart, being, mind and strength, and adds love of neighbor. The scribe agrees that these are worth more than all sacrifices, and Jesus tells him he is not far from the kingdom of God (12:28–34). Jesus asks how the Messiah can be David's son when David calls him Lord (12:35–37), warns against scribes who show off and devour widows' houses (12:38–40), and points out a poor widow who puts her last two coins into the treasury (12:41–44).
readings: Read as a contest of honor

In the ancient world public questions were challenges, and a teacher's honor depended on his answers. Read this way, chapter 12 is a series of challenges by every group of Jerusalem's leaders, each of which Jesus wins, until "no one dared to question him any longer" (12:34).
Read as a summary of Jesus' teaching

The chapter touches the great questions: Israel's history with God (the vineyard), the state (Caesar), life after death (the resurrection), the heart of the Law (the two commandments), the Messiah (David's son), and true giving (the widow). Read this way, it is Jesus' last public teaching in Mark, a compact creed.
Read as the end of the temple

The parable of the vineyard, the scribe who puts love above sacrifice, and the widow who gives all to a temple about to be torn down (13:2) all point beyond the temple. Read this way, chapter 12 prepares for chapter 13.

views.H: Each questioner represents a real group in Jerusalem: the high-priestly leaders and elders (the Sanhedrin), the Pharisees with the Herodians (supporters of Herod's family), the Sadducees (the priestly aristocracy), and a scribe. The census tax had been a flash point since AD 6, when Judas the Galilean led a revolt against it. The silver denarius bore the emperor's image, which many Jews regarded as an idol in the holy city. The Mishnah remembers thirteen offering chests in the temple, probably in the Court of the Women.
views.C: Matthew and Luke follow this sequence closely (Matthew 21:33–22:46; Luke 20:9–21:4). Matthew makes the scribe of 12:28 a hostile lawyer, drops the Shema's opening line, and expands the warning against the scribes into chapter 23; Luke moves the great commandment to another setting (Luke 10:25–28) and keeps the widow. The parable of the tenants also appears in the Gospel of Thomas (saying 65) in a shorter form, without the echo of Isaiah 5, and with the stone saying given separately (saying 66). Some scholars take Thomas as closer to Jesus' own telling; others think it shortens the Synoptic versions. Mark's explanations of Latin coin values (12:42) and the Latin word census (12:14) are often cited for a Roman setting.
views.L: The temple controversies (11:27–12:37) mirror the five controversies in Galilee (2:1–3:6), and they end, as those did, with opponents silenced. Jesus asks the last question (12:35–37), as he asked the first (11:30). The chapter is framed by two pictures of greed and generosity: the tenants who seize what is not theirs (12:7), and the widow who gives everything she has (12:44). The dearly loved son (12:6) recalls the voice at the baptism (1:11) and on the mountain (9:7).
views.J: Much of this chapter is Jesus taking sides in debates among Jews. With the Pharisees, he affirms the resurrection against the Sadducees and argues it from the Torah, as the rabbis later did (Babylonian Talmud, Sanhedrin 90b). With the friendly scribe, he places the Shema and love of neighbor at the center, as Hillel and Akiva did. Jewish scholars note that the parable of the tenants, read for centuries as God's rejection of the Jews, is aimed in Mark at the temple leadership (12:12), not at the people, who protect Jesus.
views.T: "Render to Caesar" has been the starting point of Christian teaching on church and state, from Tertullian to Augustine's two cities and Luther's two kingdoms. The Shema of 12:29 is quoted in the Catechism of the Catholic Church (202) as the faith of Israel and of the church, and it was central in the Trinitarian debates (see the card). The widow's two coins became a byword for small but costly gifts ("the widow's mite"), and the parable of the tenants was read by the fathers as the history of salvation from the prophets to Christ.

deep.b:
Between the parable of the tenants and the warning against the scribes, Mark sets four questions: about the tax (12:13–17), the resurrection (12:18–27), the greatest commandment (12:28–34) and David's son (12:35–37). David Daube noticed that they match four kinds of question that the Babylonian Talmud lists as asked of a rabbi: a question of law, a question of mockery, a question of conduct, and a question of interpretation where two Scriptures seem to conflict (Babylonian Talmud, Niddah 69b–71a). The Passover Haggadah has a similar set of four sons who ask four kinds of questions. Daube suggested that the Gospel tradition shaped this section on a pattern Jewish readers would recognize, perhaps from Passover itself, which was days away.

Whether or not the pattern is deliberate, the series shows Jesus answering each group of Jerusalem's leaders on its own ground, and then asking the question that none of them can answer: who the Messiah really is (12:35–37). That question is answered at his trial, where he quotes Psalm 110 again (14:62).

deep.h: The vineyard parable and its later use
deep.b:
For most of Christian history the parable of the tenants was read as a summary of salvation history: the slaves are the prophets, the son is Christ, the farmers are the Jewish people, and the "others" are the Gentile church. That reading fed the teaching that God had rejected the Jews, and with it centuries of contempt, which the Catholic Church formally repudiated in Nostra Aetate (1965) and many Protestant churches in later statements.

Mark's text is narrower. The parable is told to the chief priests, scribes and elders (11:27), who recognize that it is "aimed at them" (12:12), while the crowd, also Jewish, protects Jesus. The vineyard, Israel, is not destroyed; its caretakers are replaced. Many scholars, Jewish and Christian, now read it as a prophetic warning to the temple leadership, in the tradition of Isaiah 5 and of Ezekiel 34, where God condemns the shepherds and keeps the flock. Mark's first readers, after AD 70, could see that the high priesthood had in fact lost the vineyard. See also the card on Matthew 21:43.

echoes: Isaiah 5:1–7; Psalm 118:22–23; Genesis 22:2; Deuteronomy 25:5–6; Exodus 3:6; Deuteronomy 6:4–5; Leviticus 19:18; 1 Samuel 15:22; Hosea 6:6; Psalm 110:1; Exodus 22:22; Matthew 21:33–23:14; Luke 20:9–21:4; Luke 10:25–28; Romans 13:7; Acts 23:8; 14:62

settings.what: The parable of the tenants of the vineyard
settings.to: the chief priests, scribes and elders who had questioned his authority (11:27), with the crowd present
settings.when: in the temple courts, the third day in Jerusalem
settings.why: To answer the leaders' question about his authority with a story: the vineyard's owner has sent servant after servant and finally his own son, and the tenants will be judged. It warns the temple leaders that their rejection of God's messengers, now of Jesus himself, will cost them the vineyard.
settings.readers: Mark's readers heard the history of the prophets, of Jesus' death and of the fall of the temple's leaders, and the promise that the rejected stone was now the head of the corner.
views: Mark's own setting: the farmers are the temple authorities (12:12).
The traditional Christian reading: the farmers are Israel and the others the church; see the deep dive and the card on Matthew 21:43.

settings.what: The question about the tax to Caesar
settings.to: Jesus, in the temple courts
settings.when: the same day, after the parable
settings.why: A trap: "no" would be sedition reported by Herod's party, "yes" would turn the crowd, who hated the Roman tax, against him. Jesus' answer gives Caesar his coin and claims for God what bears God's image.
settings.readers: Mark's readers in the empire, who paid Rome's taxes and might be asked to honor the emperor as divine, learned that Caesar's claims were real but limited.

settings.to: Jesus, in the temple courts
settings.when: the same day
settings.why: The Sadducees, who denied the resurrection and accepted only the written Torah, use the law of the brother-in-law's duty to make resurrection look absurd. Jesus answers from God's power (the raised do not marry) and from the Torah itself (God is the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob).
settings.readers: For Mark's church, many of whose members had died or would die for their faith, the answer was a promise: God is God of the living.

settings.to: a scribe who had heard the debate, in the temple courts, with the crowd present
settings.when: the same day, after the Sadducees' question
settings.why: A sincere question about the heart of the Law, a question Jewish teachers also asked. Jesus answers with the Shema and Leviticus 19:18, and the scribe's agreement shows Jesus and a teacher of Israel at one on the center of the Torah. Matthew makes the questioner a lawyer testing Jesus (Matthew 22:35); Luke sets a similar exchange much earlier, on the road, where a lawyer gives the answer and Jesus tells the parable of the Samaritan (Luke 10:25–37).
settings.readers: For Mark's mostly Gentile church, the scene taught the confession of one God and the love that sums up the Law, and showed a scribe near the kingdom.

settings.to: the crowd in the temple, about the scribes' teaching
settings.when: while teaching in the temple, after his questioners fell silent
settings.why: To make his hearers think about who the Messiah is: not only a son of David restoring his kingdom (11:10), but David's Lord, seated at God's right hand.
settings.readers: Mark's readers confessed Jesus as Lord and heard the answer to the riddle in Jesus' words at his trial (14:62).

settings.to: the large crowd, as part of his teaching
settings.when: in the temple courts
settings.why: To warn the people against teachers who seek honor and exploit the vulnerable while praying at length, and to declare that they will be judged more strictly. Matthew expands the warning into a whole speech to the crowds and the disciples (Matthew 23).
settings.readers: Mark's church had its own teachers and leaders; the warning applied to them as well.

settings.to: his disciples, called over to watch
settings.when: sitting opposite the temple treasury, before leaving the temple for the last time (13:1)
settings.why: To show the disciples true giving, measured by cost, not size; and, many think, to show the cost of a system that let the scribes "eat up widows' houses" (12:40).
settings.readers: Mark's readers, many of them poor, heard that God sees the small gift; and, reading on into chapter 13, they saw that the temple she gave to would not stand.
views: Jesus grieves that she was drained by the temple system (Addison Wright).

traditions.q: Jesus says the first commandment is "Listen, Israel: The Lord is our God. The Lord is one" (12:29). Does the oneness of God allow belief in the Trinity?
views: Yes. Jesus affirms the Shema and confesses that God is "the one Lord" (Catechism 202); the church confesses one God in three persons, Father, Son and Holy Spirit, who share one divine nature (Catechism 253–254).

Yes. The one God is the Father, the single source from whom the Son is begotten and the Spirit proceeds; Father, Son and Spirit are one in essence and three persons. The Shema is fulfilled, not set aside.

Yes. "In the unity of the Godhead there be three persons, of one substance, power, and eternity" (Westminster Confession 2.3). Most Protestant churches, Lutheran, Anglican, Methodist and Baptist, hold the same in their confessions.
No, not as three persons. "The Lord is one" means one person. Father, Son and Holy Spirit are titles or manifestations of the one God, who is fully revealed in Jesus.
No. The one God of the Shema is Jehovah, the Father alone. Jesus quotes it as a worshiper of God, and as God's Son he is a created being, distinct from and less than the Father.
No. Jesus here repeats the Jewish creed that God is one, without adding persons. Unitarians since the Racovian Catechism (1605) have cited this verse for the oneness of God against the Trinity.

Father, Son and Holy Ghost are three distinct beings, one in purpose and will, not in substance; the Father and the Son have bodies (Doctrine and Covenants 130:22). The Shema is read as the unity of the Godhead in purpose.
